#Determine movements at a point provided
def check_movements(matrix,point):
    n_values =[]
    row,col=point
    
    for r_move, c_move in movements:
        row_get = row + r_move
        col_get = col + c_move
    
        if 0<=row_get<=(height_21_21-1) and 0<=col_get<=width_21_21-1:
            value = int(matrix[row_get, col_get])
            n_values.append(((row_get,col_get),value))            
    return n_values

#Determine if any adjcent elements contain a wall and what moves are valid
def valid_movements_check(movements):
    valid_movements = [points[0] for points in movements if points[1] == 0]
    return valid_movements

#Generate a function to keep track of unique movements to enable backtracking conditions
#Set starting point as the first movement in movement_log
movement_log = [starting_point]
def movement_tracker(movement_log, point):
    if point not in movement_log:
        movement_log.append(point)
    return movement_log

#Identify what unexplored moves are available for backtracking conditions
def unexplored_movements(valid_moves, movement_log):
    unexplored = [point for point in valid_moves if point not in movement_log]
    return unexplored
    
#Choose first available movement if possible and not explored
#Set start point as the first point in the path explored
current_path = [starting_point]
def next_movement(unexplored, current_path):    
    if unexplored:
        next_point = unexplored[0]
        current_path.append(next_point)
        return next_point

    #If no unexplored movements exist, backtrack
    else:
        print("No next movements available - backtrack one step")

        #Go one step back and remove the current position from the path
        current_path.pop()

        #Return to the previous position
        if current_path:
            return current_path[-1]

        #No movements remaining to explore
        return None

#For Las Vegas approach - generate a random next movement with wall constraints
def random_movement(valid_moves):

    #Check if any movements are available
    if not valid_moves:
        return None

    #Randomly select a valid movement
    random_index = np.random.randint(0, len(valid_moves))
    next_move = valid_moves[random_index]

    return next_move



Backtracking function
Coding question 1.b.ii
We predfine the movements based on the assignment criteria, where the only allowed movements are up/down/left/right as stored in the movements list
Before taking a next step, the backtracking function will first determine what movements are avaible by calling the check_movements and valid_movements_check functions. These function ensure the next possible move is either up/down/left/right and not moving outside of the matrix, i.e. staying within the borders of the maze. Hence only keeping positions where movement is possible
Since we have defined movements as [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)], the function will first check if going up is possible, if not it will check if down movement is possible,followed by left and lastly right.
The movement_tracker function stores and keeps track of the unique locations visited as we move through the matrix, by using the movement_log.
The unexplored_movements function will check if any of the results from valid_movements_check has been visited yet, if it has not been visisted yet, assign it to the unexplored list, this ensures that previously visisted locations are not selected again when moving forward with a next movement.
The next_movement function will take the element from unexplored array and assign it as the next location to move to. The selected location is also added to current_path which keeps track of the current route taken so far .
If no movements are available, i.e. unexplored is any empty list, then pop the last element from current_path, essentially removing the last position from the list and moving one step back, which follows a Last-In, First-Out approach. In the latter case, we have added the location to the movement_log so this location can not be visited again when calling the unexplored_movements function
This process will repeat with the loop in place until either the exit point is reached or if we no more unexplored options. Having an empty unexplored will stop the algorithm since we will first attempt to move one step back to previous location, only when* current_path becomes an empty list then* next_movement will return a null/none value, in which case the loop will break.
This approach follows a depth-first search as observed in DSA-1, where it explores a branch as far as possible before moving back to explore other branches



Use modular functions as defined above

In [7]:
#Possible movement (up/down/left/right) at any given point
movements = [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]

def backtracking(matrix,starting_point,exit_point):

    #Set initial conditions
    movement_log = [starting_point]
    movement_all_log = [starting_point]
    current_path = [starting_point]
    current_point = starting_point
    moves=0
    success_count = 0
    
    while current_point != exit_point:
    
        #Step1 Find possible movements
        possible_moves = check_movements(matrix, current_point)
    
        #Step2 Find valid movements
        valid_moves = valid_movements_check(possible_moves)
    
        #Step3 Remove explored movements
        unexplored = unexplored_movements(valid_moves, movement_log)
    
        #Step4 Select next movement
        previous_path_length = len(current_path)
        next_point = next_movement(unexplored, current_path)
        if len(current_path) < previous_path_length:
            print(f"Backtracking to {next_point}")
            current_point = next_point
        
        #Stop if no movements remain
        if next_point is None:
            break
            
        #Step5 Log movement
        movement_all_log.append(next_point)
        movement_tracker(movement_log, next_point)
    
        if current_point != next_point:
            print(f"current point: {current_point} and move to next point {next_point}")
        #Update current point
        current_point = next_point
        moves=moves+1

        if current_point == exit_point:
            success_count += 1
            
    return {
    "moves": moves,
    "movement_log": movement_log,
    "movement_all_log": movement_all_log,
    "current_path": current_path,
    "path_length": len(current_path),
    "success_count": success_count,
    }



Las Vegas function
Coding question 1.b.i
The las_vegas function will attempt 200 movements or stop if the exit point is reached before 200 moves - as seen in the while loop process in the function below

Use modular functions as defined above

In [8]:
def las_vegas(matrix, starting_point, exit_point):

    #Set initial conditions
    movement_log = [starting_point]
    movement_all_log = [starting_point]
    current_point = starting_point
    moves = 0
    success_count = 0

    #Max 200 moves allowed or until exist is found
    while current_point != exit_point and moves < 200:

        #Step1 Find possible movements
        possible_moves = check_movements(matrix, current_point)

        #Step2 Find valid movements
        valid_moves = valid_movements_check(possible_moves)

        #Step3 Randomly select next movement with wall conditions applied
        next_point = random_movement(valid_moves)

        #Stop if no valid movements exist
        if next_point is None:
            break

        #Step4 Log movement
        movement_all_log.append(next_point)
        movement_tracker(movement_log, next_point)

        #Step5 Update current position
        current_point = next_point
        moves += 1

    #Keep track successful exists
    if current_point == exit_point:
        success_count += 1

    return {
        "success_count": success_count,
        "moves": moves,
        "movement_log": movement_log,
        "movement_all_log": movement_all_log
    }



Generate movement GIF function

In [9]:
#Function to generate an animation to show the movements of the algorithm
def generate_maze_gif(matrix, movement_all_log, algorithm, starting_point, exit_point, fps=4):

    history = np.array(movement_all_log)

    #create/Overwrite file
    gif_filename = f"maze_{algorithm.lower().replace(' ', '_')}.gif"

    #Generate maze
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))
    ax.imshow(matrix, cmap="gray_r")

    #Create movement points
    trail, = ax.plot([], [], "b.-", linewidth=2,markersize=4, label="Movement history")

    current_dot, = ax.plot([], [], "ro", markersize=8,label="Current position")

    #Indicate entrance and exit
    ax.plot(starting_point[1], starting_point[0],"go", markersize=9, label="Entrance")

    ax.plot(exit_point[1], exit_point[0],"mo", markersize=9, label="Exit")

    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.legend()

    #Plot movement point for each frame
    def update(frame):
        path_so_far = history[:frame + 1]

        #Columns
        x = path_so_far[:, 1]
        #Rows
        y = path_so_far[:, 0] 

        trail.set_data(x, y)
        current_dot.set_data([x[-1]], [y[-1]])

        ax.set_title(f"{algorithm} - Movement {frame}")

        return trail, current_dot

    #Generate gif for each frame
    gif = FuncAnimation(
        fig,
        update,
        frames=len(history),
        interval=1000 / fps,
        blit=False,
        repeat=False
    )

    
    gif.save(gif_filename, writer=PillowWriter(fps=fps))
    plt.close(fig)

    return gif_filename

Backtracking vs Las Vegas Comparison¶

What is the difference between Backtracking and Las Vegas
The main difference between the Backtracking and Las Vegas alogrithm is how the next movement is selected and how previously visited locations are handled. Both alogrithms have the same movement restrictions, being only able to move one step up/down/left/right and are not allowed to move outside of the maze border

Backtracking: The Backtracking approach follows a predefined order of movements, where the first available unexplored movement is selected based on the movements list, prioritising up, down, left and right (these are the defined movements in this specfic order).
This approach ensures that the algorithm explores the maze without repeatedly exploring the same locations.
The algorithm will continue until the exit is found or all possible routes have been explored.

Las Vegas: The Las Vegas approach does not follow a predefined movement with priority when selecting the next position. Instead it randomly selects one of the available movements (given the movement criteria of up/down/left/right and must stay within the border).
This randomized movement selection process can result in a location being explored multiple times and also allows the algorithm to explore the same movement patterns that was already explored. So this can result in the algorithm spending a large number of movements exploring the same area of the maze, rather than progressing towards the exit.
The Las Vegas approach also has a maximum limit of 200 movements (as specified in the assignment). The algorithm will be successful if the exit is reached within the 200 movements, otherwise it will be unsuccessful once the movement limit has been reached.

Which data structure/s would you use to implement this problem?¶

NumPy Array:
Converting an image to array - The maze is initially imported from the PNG image and then converted into a binary NumPy array.
The array stores the maze structure where 0 represents a walkable path and 1 represents a wall.
This also allows the functions to access specific locations within the maze using row and column as "coordinates".
NumPy array also enables to interpret the maze image as a two-dimensional grid/matrix which allows to identify explored-, next-, valid- and invalid movements

Python Lists/Tuples:
Python lists are used throughout both algorithms to store available movements, explored locations, unexplored locations and the sequence of steps as you move through the maze.
The movements list stores the predefined movement directions as tuples (in a specific order of (-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)).
Lists were chosen since they are easy to update using functions such as append() and allows iterations and compare the available movements against previously visited positions.

Last-in, First-out Stacks:
For the Backtracking approach, the current_path list is used as a stack, following LIFO principle.
When moving to a next location, the next position is added to current_path using append(). If no unexplored movements are available, the function uses pop() to remove the most recently added position and move one step backwards.

Dictionary:
Both algorithms return the results using a Python dictionary, containing values such as succesful exits, all movements log and unique movements. This also makes it easier to compare results of both the backtracking and Las Vegas algorithm

Backtracking vs Las Vegas Comparison success rate after 10 000 runs¶

In [27]:
#Generate function to compare succesful run comparison

import contextlib
import io

def test_success_rate(matrix, starting_point, exit_point, total_runs=10000):

    backtracking_successes = 0
    las_vegas_successes = 0

    for run in range(total_runs):

        #Avoid printing each movement
        with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
            #Backtracking
            backtracking_result = backtracking(matrix, starting_point, exit_point)
            
            #Las Vegas
            las_vegas_result = las_vegas(matrix, starting_point, exit_point)
            
        #Track succesful exists
        backtracking_successes += backtracking_result["success_count"]
        las_vegas_successes += las_vegas_result["success_count"]
        
    #success rates
    backtracking_rate = (backtracking_successes / total_runs) * 100
    las_vegas_rate = (las_vegas_successes / total_runs) * 100

    return {
        "total_runs": total_runs,
        "backtracking_successes": backtracking_successes,
        "las_vegas_successes": las_vegas_successes,
        "backtracking_rate": backtracking_rate,
        "las_vegas_rate": las_vegas_rate
    }

#Execute function
results = test_success_rate(maze_grid,starting_point,exit_point,total_runs=10000)



print("Backtracking performance:")
print("Total Backtracking runs:", results["total_runs"])
print("Successful Backtracking runs:", results["backtracking_successes"])
print(f"Backtracking success rate: {results['backtracking_rate']:.2f}%")
print("\n")
print("Las Vegas performance (max200 movements):")
print("Total Las Vegas runs:", results["total_runs"])
print("Successful Las Vegas runs:", results["las_vegas_successes"])
print(f"Las Vegas success rate: {results['las_vegas_rate']:.2f}%")

Successful Las Vegas runs: 0

Key observations:

Backtracking:
Since backtracking follows a predefined movement priority, the success rate for each run will be exactly same.
If the first run will be successfull then all consecutive runs will be succesfull as well, the opposite is also true, if the first run is unsucessfull then all consecutive runs will be unsucessfull.
In the this case, the first run was successfull so we have a 100% success rate for all 10 000 runs.

Las Vegas:
Las Vegas algorithm randomly selects the next available movement using the np.random.randint() function. This means the algorithm can repeatedly apply the exact same movement pattern without effectively "move forward".
Additional the run will be defined as unsuccesfull if it reaches the 200 movement limit
In this case of 10 000 runs, 0 runs executed successfully, resulting in a 0% success rate.

Based on this outcome, we can conclude that backtracking is the more effective algorithm to successfully exit the maze since it avoids repeating movement sequences.

Coding 2.b.a: Kruskal's MST
Create Kruskal's MST algorithm (greedy algorithm)
Greedy algorithms works in a way by selecting the optimal choice at each immediate step, i.e. thinking “locally”, considering only the next best step at the current point and not the best step for the bigger picture (not “globally”)

Coding 2.b.b: Create function to execute Kruskal's MST algorithm

In [42]:
def MyMinimumSpanningTree(Graph) -> nx.Graph:
    #Set an empty graph with our predefined nodes
    kruskal = nx.Graph()
    kruskal.add_nodes_from(Graph.nodes())

    #Sort edges from smallest to largest weights
    #NetworkX output structure (node_from,node_to,{weight: val}
    #NetworkX output structure - dictionary: first element[from_node], second element [to_node], third element tuple of variable and value {'weight',value}
    sorted_edges = sorted(Graph.edges(data=True), key=lambda edge: edge[2]["weight"])
    
    #Create a loop to sort the edges from smallest to largest weights
    for step, (start, end, data) in enumerate(sorted_edges, start=1):
        weight = data["weight"]

        #Check if nodes are connected
        if nx.has_path(kruskal,start,end):
            #If already exists remove to avoid loop between same nodes
            print(f"Step {step}: {start} -> {end} with weight: {weight}  (remove)")
        else:
            kruskal.add_edge(start,end,weight=weight)
            print(f"Step {step}: {start} -> {end} with weight: {weight} (add)")

    return kruskal

kruskal_result = MyMinimumSpanningTree(graph)

Task 3 Recursion algorithms:¶

Create a function that receives a list of strings. Each string can be either “blue”, “red” or “green”.
The goal is to move through the list incrementing the index by following the instructions below:
If the string at index i is “blue”, the next element is the element following the next appearance of the string “blue”.
If the string at index i is “red”, the next element is the element in the index 2x(i) + 1.
If the string at index i is “green”, the next element is the following element in the list, i.e. at the index i+1



Task3 a: Code the function using recursion

In [80]:
def follow_instructions(instructions: list[str]) -> list[int]:

    #recursive function to check the list
    def index_checker(i):

        #create a stop function as requirement of recursive function
        if i >= len(instructions):
            print("stop condition envoked - index greater or same as instruction list")
            return []

        #Check current colour at the index i
        current_colour = instructions[i]
        print(f"current index {i}: and current colour: {current_colour}")

        #If the string at index i is “blue”, the next element is the element following the next appearance of the string “blue”. 
        if current_colour == "blue":
            print(f"current colour: {current_colour}, apply rules for blue")
            try:
                #find the next "blue" index then return the index after that element
                blue_next = instructions.index("blue", i + 1)
                find_index = blue_next + 1
                print(f"next index: {find_index}")
            except ValueError:
                print("No further blue colours found")
                return[i]
                
        #If the string at index i is “red”, the next element is the element in the index 2x(i) + 1. 
        elif current_colour == "red":
            print(f"current colour: {current_colour}, apply rules for {current_colour}")
            find_index = (2 * i) + 1

        #If the string at index i is “green”, the next element is the following element in the list
        else:
            print(f"current colour: green, apply rules for green")
            find_index= i + 1
            print(f"next index: {find_index}")

        #Return current and new index based on the conditions
        return[i] + index_checker(find_index)

    return index_checker(0)

current colour: red, apply rules for red

Task 5 Unit 6.2:¶

Question 6.2.a:

Cat Swarm Optimization:
Tracking behaviour: Consiously following and movings towards a target, moving according to it's own velocities for every dimension. With each move, it updates it's own velocity and position towards the best solution identified up until that point

Seeking behaviour: Resting behaviour, while aware of surroundings, may or may not move to a different location.
The are four factors to consider in seeking behaviour:
Seeking memory pool (SMP): Define the size of the seeking memory for each cat.
Seeking range of the selected dimensions (SRD): Declares the mutative ratio for the selected dimensions.
Counts of dimension to change(CDC) : Indicates how many dimensions will be varied.
Self-position considering (SPC): Boolean variable, which decides whether the point the cat is already standing at will be one of the candidates to move to


Grey Wolf Optimization:
The algorithm creates wolves into four groups, Alpha, Beta, Delta and Omega, where the Alpha wolf is the best solution indetified so far and Omega wolf is the all other remaining solutions after Alpha, Beta and Delta wolves.
Approaching the prey:
Search according to the position of the alpha, beta and delta. Diverge from each other to search for prey and then converge to attack prey. Essentially exploring multiple different possible solutions instead of focusing on one singular location

Encircling the prey:
Guided by the Alpha (best solution identified so far), the Beta and Delta wolves will adjust their position to the Alpha, converging to the best possible solution identified at this point.

Attacking the prey:
As progressing, the algorithm/wolves focus more closely on the best solution identified so far, it will attempt improve best idenitified solution instead of keep searching for other solutions. The is finished when prey is attacked and when the algorithm/wolves stop moving.
